steps.step: A bit in a filter is 1 exactly when at least one added item hashes to that position. Otherwise it stays 0.
steps.part: The parts; How it works (step 1, Add); Why "no" is always right
steps.idea: All bits start at 0. Adding an item sets its k positions to 1, and nothing ever sets a bit back to 0. So the final array is just the union of all the positions the added items hash to.

steps.step: The two filters are comparable position by position, and an item's positions are the same in both.
steps.part: The parts (hash functions: the same item always gives the same position)
steps.idea: Same m and same hash functions means each item maps to the same k positions in either filter.

steps.step: A bitwise OR of the two arrays gives a bit of 1 exactly where some item of A or some item of B set it. That is the set of positions covered by A ∪ B.
steps.idea: OR switches a bit on if either input bit is on, and that matches 'some item in A ∪ B hashes here'.

steps.step: So the OR is exactly the same array you would get by adding every item of A ∪ B to an empty filter. It is exact: no information is lost compared with building it from the items. It still has the normal false-positive behaviour of a filter holding |A ∪ B| items.
steps.part: Step 3; How "yes" can be wrong; How much memory, and how often wrong
steps.idea: Same bits means same answers. False positives come from bit overlap and grow with how full the filter is, and the union filter holds more items.

steps.step: A bitwise AND keeps a bit on only where it is on in both filters. Every item in A ∩ B has all its bits on in both filters, so AND keeps them all. A query for an item in A ∩ B is still 'probably yes', so there are no false negatives for the intersection.
steps.part: Step 1; Why "no" is always right; background (AND)
steps.idea: Bits of items in both sets are 1 in both arrays, so they survive the AND.

steps.step: But a bit can be on in both filters because of different items: some a in A only and some b in B only can share a position, just as cat and dog share bit 6. The AND then keeps bits that no item of A ∩ B ever set. So the result can have more 1s than a filter built directly from A ∩ B. It is not exact, and its false-positive rate can be higher. An item in only one set can even pass if each of its bits is on in both filters.
steps.part: How it works (cat and dog both set bit 6); How "yes" can be wrong (the filter cannot tell which item set a bit)
steps.idea: Bits do not record which item set them, so the AND cannot separate 'set by a shared item' from 'set by different items that happen to collide'.

result: To get A ∪ B, take the bitwise OR of the two arrays. This is exact: it is bit for bit the filter you would get by adding all items of A ∪ B, with that filter's usual false-positive rate. The bitwise AND gives a filter for A ∩ B that never says 'no' to an item really in both sets. It is not exact, though: bits set by different items in A and in B can coincide, so it may have extra 1s compared with a filter built from A ∩ B. That means more false positives. It is a superset approximation of the true intersection filter.
